lead: Baseband data transmission means sending a stream of bits as pulses through a cable or any low-pass channel, and getting the same bits back at the far end. This unit explains why fast pulses spill into their neighbours, how to shape and equalise them, how to picture signals as points in space, and how a matched filter with a nearest-point decision gives the smallest possible error rate. After it you can compute the Nyquist bandwidth of a link, design a raised cosine or duobinary scheme, and write the probability of error for binary and M-ary PAM.
about: The unit follows one bit stream from the transmitter's pulse shaper to the receiver's decision. It starts with why pulses sent close together spill into each other and the Nyquist condition that stops it, makes that condition practical with the raised cosine pulse and reads the result on an eye pattern, and repairs a channel that spoils the pulse with an equalizer. It then turns waveforms into points in a signal space, shows that the matched filter is the best front end, and computes the error probability of the optimum detector in white Gaussian noise. It ends with two ways to send faster in a given band: duobinary signalling and M-ary PAM.

chapters.idea: When pulses are sent faster than their tails die out, each sample carries bits of its neighbours, and Nyquist's criterion says exactly when that spill is zero.
chapters.depth: Build the model: symbols aₖ from an alphabet, one every T seconds, so the symbol rate is R_s = 1/T baud; transmit filter g_T(t), channel c(t), receive filter g_R(t). The overall pulse is p(t) = g_T(t) * c(t) * g_R(t). Write the sample as y(kT) = aₖp(0) + Σ over n≠k of aₙ p((k−n)T) + noise, and name the middle sum the intersymbol interference (ISI). Define peak distortion as the worst-case ISI divided by p(0). State Nyquist's first criterion, also called the zero-ISI condition: p(nT) = 0 for every integer n ≠ 0. Show that it needs at least R_s/2 Hz of bandwidth, so an ideal binary link tops out at 2 bit/s/Hz, and that the pulse meeting it exactly is the sinc, p(t) = sinc(t/T), which is non-causal and infinitely long. Use the figure to show sinc pulses whose zero crossings land on the other sampling instants.

figure.aria: Two sinc pulses one symbol period apart, and their sum, which passes through 1 at each sampling instant because the other pulse is exactly zero there.

chapters.example: A binary source sends 2400 bit/s using Nyquist pulses. The overall pulse has p(0) = 1 and p(±T) = 0.25, and the neighbouring symbols are aₖ₋₁ = +1, aₖ = −1, aₖ₊₁ = +1. Find the symbol rate, the minimum bandwidth, and the sampled value. Binary, so R_s = R_b = 2400 baud and T = 1/2400 s = 416.7 µs. Minimum bandwidth = R_s/2 = 1200 Hz. Sample = (−1)(1) + (+1)(0.25) + (+1)(0.25) = −0.5, so the ISI of +0.5 is half the wanted amplitude of 1 and has pushed the sample a long way towards the decision threshold.
chapters.trap: Using R_s where R_s/2 belongs, and mixing bit rate with symbol rate: for M levels, R_b = R_s log₂M. ISI is set by the overall response g_T * c * g_R, never by the transmit filter alone.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for the Fourier transform and power spectral density; Unit 4 for line codes and the idea of a symbol period.
chapters.leave: Raised cosine design goes to 5.2, equaliser design to 5.3, and ISI inside a passband system to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The raised cosine pulse meets Nyquist's zero-ISI condition with a finite, gradual spectrum, paying a controlled extra bandwidth that the eye pattern lets you see and measure.
chapters.depth: Start from the ideal sinc's rectangular spectrum and round its corners with a cosine roll-off of factor α, 0 ≤ α ≤ 1, called the roll-off factor, also called the excess bandwidth factor. Give the bandwidth B = (R_s/2)(1 + α), the excess bandwidth αR_s/2, and the two extremes: α = 0 is the sinc, α = 1 gives B = R_s with the fastest decaying tails, roughly 1/t³. Quote the time-domain form p(t) = sinc(t/T) · cos(παt/T) / (1 − (2αt/T)²) without deriving it. Explain the practical split into a root raised cosine filter at the transmitter and a matched root raised cosine at the receiver, whose cascade is the raised cosine. Then the eye pattern, also called the eye diagram: overlay two symbol periods of the received waveform for many symbol sequences. Read the eye opening as the noise margin, the horizontal opening as the timing margin against jitter, the slope at the zero crossing as timing sensitivity, and a closing eye as growing ISI.

figure.title: Where the raised cosine is made
figure.aria: The data passes through a root raised cosine transmit filter, the channel and a matched receive filter, so the overall pulse seen by the sampler is a raised cosine whose eye is measured at the end.

chapters.example: Binary data at 4800 bit/s goes through a raised cosine system with α = 0.5. Find the symbol rate, symbol period, bandwidth and excess bandwidth. Binary, so R_s = 4800 baud, T = 1/4800 s = 208.3 µs. Nyquist bandwidth = R_s/2 = 2400 Hz. Actual bandwidth = 2400 × (1 + 0.5) = 3600 Hz. Excess bandwidth = 3600 − 2400 = 1200 Hz, which is αR_s/2. With α = 1 the same link would need 4800 Hz.
chapters.trap: Choosing α = 0 because it is the narrowest. The sinc is not realisable and its tails decay so slowly that a small timing error floods the sample with ISI; practical links use α near 0.2 to 0.5. Also, do not read the eye at its widest point in time, but at the instant the sampler actually fires.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for the zero-ISI condition and the sinc pulse.
chapters.leave: Equalisers that repair a damaged pulse go to 5.3; eye-mask specifications for passband radio belong to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: An equaliser is a tapped delay line at the receiver whose weights are set to cancel the channel's ISI, either by inverting the channel exactly or by adapting from the data itself.
chapters.depth: Show that a channel spreads each pulse over several symbol periods and that the receiver can undo this with a linear transversal equaliser: a delay line with taps spaced T, weights c₋ₙ … cₙ, and a summing node. Zero-forcing (ZF), also called the inverse filter: choose the weights so the overall sampled response is 1 at k = 0 and 0 at every other k, which in the frequency domain is C(f) = 1/H(f). Write the tap equations as a set of linear equations, solved by matrix inversion or by the iterative zero-forcing algorithm. State the price: where |H(f)| is small the equaliser gain is large, so noise is amplified, and at a spectral null the ZF filter is impossible. Name the minimum mean-square error equaliser as the cure, in one line. Then adaptive equalisers: the channel is unknown and drifts, so the weights are updated by the LMS rule c_k(n+1) = c_k(n) + μ e(n) x(n−k), where μ is the step size, e(n) = d(n) − â(n) is the error, d(n) is the known training symbol, and x(n−k) is the stored input. Explain training mode, then decision-directed mode, plus the trade-off: large μ converges fast but jitters, small μ is steady but slow.

figure.title: Adaptive linear equaliser
figure.aria: The received samples pass down a delay line, are weighted and summed to a decision, and the resulting error is fed back with the LMS rule to change the weights.

chapters.example: A channel has sampled response h₀ = 1, h₁ = 0.5, h₂ = 0.25 and zero elsewhere. Find a two-tap zero-forcing equaliser and the residual ISI. Put c₀ = 1/h₀ = 1 and c₁ = −h₁/h₀² = −0.5. Check the overall response v_k = Σ c_j h_{k−j}: v₀ = c₀h₀ = 1; v₁ = c₀h₁ + c₁h₀ = 0.5 − 0.5 = 0; v₂ = c₀h₂ + c₁h₁ = 0.25 − 0.25 = 0; v₃ = c₁h₂ = −0.125. So the two post-cursors at T and 2T are cancelled and one small residual of −0.125 is left at 3T.
chapters.trap: Believing zero-forcing removes the noise as well as the ISI. It does the opposite: near a null in |H(f)| the tap gains blow up and the noise with them, which is why the ZF receiver is not the best receiver when the signal-to-noise ratio is low.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 and 5.2 for the sampled overall response and the zero-ISI target.
chapters.leave: Channel estimation, maximum-likelihood sequence detection and the Viterbi algorithm for bandlimited channels go to Unit 7; equalisation inside a passband modem belongs to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Any set of M signals of duration T can be drawn as M points in a space of at most M dimensions, and the Gram-Schmidt procedure builds the coordinate axes.
chapters.depth: Define the inner product of two real signals over one symbol interval, ⟨x, y⟩ = ∫ x(t)y(t) dt from 0 to T, the norm ‖x‖ = √⟨x, x⟩ which equals the square root of the energy, and orthonormality ⟨φᵢ, φⱼ⟩ = 1 if i = j and 0 otherwise. Write the expansion s_m(t) = Σ over i of s_mi φᵢ(t), where s_mi = ⟨s_m, φᵢ⟩ is the coordinate, and note the energy is Σ s_mi² and the squared distance between two signals is Σ (s_mi − s_ni)². Give the Gram-Schmidt steps: φ₁ = s₁/‖s₁‖; then g_m = s_m − Σ⟨s_m, φᵢ⟩φᵢ; if ‖g_m‖ = 0 the signal is linearly dependent and adds no dimension, otherwise φ_new = g_m/‖g_m‖. State that the number of dimensions N is at most M. State the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality |⟨x, y⟩| ≤ ‖x‖‖y‖, with equality only when one signal is a constant multiple of the other, and say it is the step that caps the matched filter's output. Give the 1-D picture for PAM and BPSK and the 2-D picture for QPSK.

figure.title: Gram-Schmidt in one pass
figure.aria: Each signal is projected on the axes already found, the projection is subtracted, and a non-zero leftover is normalised into a new axis; a zero leftover is skipped.

chapters.example: Over 0 ≤ t < T = 1 ms, s₁(t) = 1 V for the whole interval and s₂(t) = 2 V for the first half and 0 V for the second. Work in units of V·√ms. E₁ = 1, so φ₁ = s₁ and ‖s₁‖ = 1. Inner product ⟨s₂, φ₁⟩ = 2 × 0.5 = 1. Residual g₂ = s₂ − 1·φ₁, that is +1 over the first half and −1 over the second, so ‖g₂‖ = 1 and φ₂ = g₂. The points are s₁ = (1, 0) and s₂ = (1, 1), the distance is 1 V·√ms, and ⟨s₁, s₂⟩ = 1 ≤ √(1 × 2) = 1.414 satisfies Cauchy-Schwarz with room to spare.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that the basis size is at most M and that dependent signals must be skipped, and then using N = M in the error formula. Energy is the squared norm while squared distance is the sum of squared coordinate differences — not the difference of the two energies.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for the Fourier transform and orthogonality of sinusoids.
chapters.leave: Passband constellations such as M-PSK and QAM go to Unit 6; only the geometry is needed here.

chapters.idea: The filter that maximises the signal-to-noise ratio at the sampling instant is the signal itself, time-reversed and delayed by T, and a multiplier followed by an integrator does exactly the same job.
chapters.depth: State the problem: a known pulse s(t) of duration T arrives buried in white noise of two-sided power spectral density N₀/2; find the receive filter h(t) that maximises the ratio of peak output signal power to output noise power at t = T. Quote the answer h(t) = s(T − t) with transfer function H(f) = S*(f)e^(−j2πfT), the matched filter, also called the optimum filter for white noise. Sketch the derivation with the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality: the peak output is E, the output noise variance is N₀E/2, so the maximum signal-to-noise ratio is 2E/N₀, which equals E/(N₀/2) when the ratio is written with the one-sided density. Explain the time-reversal picture: the output is the autocorrelation of s(t) shifted to peak at t = T. Then the correlation receiver, also called the correlation detector: multiply r(t) by s(t) and integrate from 0 to T, dumping the result at t = T (integrate and dump). Show that it produces the same sample value E as the matched filter, so the two are equivalent, and note that the matched filter is convenient in hardware while the correlator is convenient in analysis.

figure.title: Two ways to build the same receiver
figure.aria: The received signal splits into a matched filter branch and a multiply-and-integrate branch; both give the same sample at t = T, which then goes to the threshold and the decision.

chapters.example: A rectangular pulse of amplitude 1 V and duration T = 1 ms is received in white noise with one-sided density N₀ = 2×10⁻⁶ W/Hz, so N₀/2 = 10⁻⁶ W/Hz. Energy E = A²T = 1 × 10⁻³ = 1 mJ. Maximum output signal-to-noise ratio = 2E/N₀ = 2(10⁻³)/(2×10⁻⁶) = 1000, which is 30 dB, an amplitude ratio of √1000 ≈ 31.6. Any other filter shape gives a smaller value at the sampling instant.
chapters.trap: Dropping the factor of two by confusing N₀ with N₀/2 and reporting E/N₀ as the answer, which is 3 dB low. Also, the matched filter maximises the ratio only at t = T; its output at other instants is not optimal, and an early or late sampling clock spoils the result.
chapters.prereq: 5.4 for the inner product and Cauchy-Schwarz; Unit 1 for white noise and power spectral density.
chapters.leave: Non-coherent and differential detection go to Unit 6; the noise figure of a receiver front end belongs to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: In white Gaussian noise the receiver with the smallest error probability compares the received point with the signal points and picks the nearest one, and the error probability depends only on how far apart the points are and on N₀.
chapters.depth: Write the received vector as r = s_m + n, where n has independent Gaussian components of variance N₀/2 per dimension. Derive the maximum-likelihood rule: pick the m that maximises ⟨r, s_m⟩ − E_m/2, which for equal energies is the same as picking the nearest point, called the minimum-distance rule. Describe decision regions as the Voronoi cells of the points, separated by perpendicular bisectors. State the error probability for two equally likely points at distance d with equal energies: P_e = Q(d/√(2N₀)), where Q(x) = (1/√(2π)) ∫ from x to infinity of e^(−u²/2) du, Q(0) = 0.5, and Q is decreasing. For antipodal binary, d = 2√E_b, so P_e = Q(√(2E_b/N₀)) = ½ erfc(√(E_b/N₀)). Extend to M-PAM: P_e = (2(M−1)/M) Q(√(6E_s/((M²−1)N₀))), where E_s is the average symbol energy. Mention the union bound for M-ary sets in one line.

figure.aria: Two signal points on a line, the dashed perpendicular bisector that separates their decision regions, and a received point on the s₂ side of the boundary.

chapters.example: Binary antipodal signalling has E_b/N₀ = 10, that is 10 dB. Then P_e = Q(√20) = Q(4.47). Using Q(4.5) = 3.4×10⁻⁶, the answer is about 4×10⁻⁶ per bit. If the link must reach P_e = 10⁻⁵ instead, solve Q(x) = 10⁻⁵, which gives x ≈ 4.27, so E_b/N₀ = x²/2 = 9.1, that is 9.6 dB — about 0.4 dB less than 10 dB.
chapters.trap: Swapping E_s and E_b and losing the 2 in the binary formula: antipodal binary gives Q(√(2E_b/N₀)), not Q(√(E_b/N₀)), and a missing 2 is a silent 3 dB error in every number that follows.
chapters.prereq: 5.5 for the matched filter sample and its noise variance; Unit 1 for the Gaussian density and AWGN.
chapters.leave: Coding gain and the error performance of coded systems go to Unit 7; fading channels and passband error rates go to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Correlative coding deliberately creates a known, small ISI so a binary stream fits a realisable Nyquist filter, while M-ary PAM raises the bit rate by sending log₂M bits on each symbol.
chapters.depth: Introduce partial response signalling, also called correlative coding. Duobinary, or class I partial response: the channel output is cₖ = aₖ + aₖ₋₁, so a binary input produces three levels 0, 1, 2 at the Nyquist bandwidth R_s/2, exactly 2 bit/s/Hz, but with a realisable filter instead of the impossible sinc. Explain the precoder: pₖ = bₖ ⊕ pₖ₋₁ before the coder, so that a single decision error does not propagate forever; the decoder is simply b̂ₖ = cₖ mod 2. State the cost: three levels instead of two roughly double the error probability for the same transmitted power, since the distance between adjacent levels is halved. Mention modified duobinary, cₖ = aₖ − aₖ₋₂, which removes the DC component, and note the polynomial names 1 + D and 1 − D². Then M-ary PAM: M levels, log₂M bits per symbol, symbol rate R_s = R_b/log₂M, bandwidth (R_s/2)(1 + α), M − 1 decision thresholds, average energy (M²−1)d²/3 for levels spaced 2d, and Gray labelling so that one symbol error costs one bit error.

figure.title: Duobinary transmitter and receiver
figure.aria: The binary stream is precoded with one bit of memory, added to its own delayed copy to make three levels, sent over the channel, decided with two thresholds, and decoded by taking the level modulo two.

chapters.example: A link must carry 9600 bit/s with a raised cosine roll-off α = 0.25. Compare binary and 4-PAM. Binary: R_s = 9600 baud, B = (9600/2)(1.25) = 6000 Hz. 4-PAM: 2 bits per symbol, so R_s = 9600/2 = 4800 baud, T = 208.3 µs, B = (4800/2)(1.25) = 3000 Hz, and the receiver needs 3 thresholds. Keeping the same spacing d between levels, average energy is (M²−1)/3 = 5 times the binary value, so half the bandwidth costs about 7 dB of power.
chapters.trap: Running duobinary without a precoder, so one wrong three-level decision corrupts every later bit. For M-ary PAM, remember M − 1 thresholds and the (M²−1)/3 power penalty; a lower symbol rate is not free.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 and 5.2 for the Nyquist bandwidth and pulse shaping; 5.6 for the error probability formula extended to M levels.
chapters.leave: Trellis-coded modulation and maximum-likelihood sequence detection go to Unit 7; M-ary PSK and QAM on a carrier belong to Unit 6.
